newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban closes Iran embassy for "spying".
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban closes Iran embassy for "spying".

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban militia government on Monday ordered the Iranian embassy in Kabul to close for alleged spying and interference in the war-shattered country's internal affairs.
The embassy was closed "temporarily" and its staff were given 48 hours to leave Afghanistan, official Kabul radio quoted an Afghan Foreign Ministry statement as saying.
Iranian state radio dismissed the charges and dismissed the Taleban's action as a form of a retaliation for its recent "heavy defeats" in northern Afghanistan.

Wakil Ahmad, a senior Taleban official in the southern city of Kandahar, told a Pakistan-based Afghan news service that the embassy had been "gathering wrong information" about Afghanistan. He said Tehran was not neutral in the Afghan conflict.
"They were involved in activities of spying," the Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) service quoted him as saying about the Iranian embassy staff.
AIP quoted Ahmad as also saying the Iranian press had been spreading misinformation about Afghanistan and Tehran was not in favour of reconciliation with the Taleban government.
Kabul radio, monitored in Islamabad, said the Afghan government had what it called undeniable evidence that Iran used its Kabul embassy staff to interfere in Afghan internal affairs.
"Therefore, the government has ordered the embassy closed until the situation becomes normal in the country and until further notice," he said.
There was no immediate information about the number of embassy staff and whether they had left Kabul.

The Iranian embassy has been among the very few diplomatic missions to remain open in Kabul throughout the factional fighting that has plagued the Afghan capital since Islamic guerrilla forces ousted a communist government in 1992.
Shi'ite Moslem Iran has been uneasy at the emergence of the purist Sunni Moslem Taleban in nearby Afghanistan.

Iran has refused to recognise the Taleban government, which was set up after the militia captured Kabul in September last year, and still regards ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani as the legitimate Afghan president.

The Afghan Foreign Ministry alleged that Iranian interference increased after recent Taleban advances in northern Afghanistan and accused Tehran of giving logistical help to Taleban's opponents and starting a propaganda war through its media.

"It should be said that following heavy defeats in different parts of Afghanistan and having lost all the areas under their control in the north of the country, and after suffering heavy loss of life, the Taleban group have been obliged to resort to such a means as a retaliatory measure," the radio said.

"Iran has said many times that it was not interfering in the internal affairs of any country, including Afghanistan, and that it always wanted peace and calm and and end to war in that country," it added.
